blocks.html: In Class 9 you wrote every program inside main() . That works for short programs, but a real program — a school result system or a shop billing program — may have thousands of lines. Writing everything in one block makes it hard to read, test and correct.
A function is a named block of code that does one particular job. You write it once and call it by name whenever you need that job done.

Think of a school canteen. The cashier does not cook; she sends the order to the kitchen, the kitchen prepares the food and sends it back. The cashier is the caller, the kitchen is the function, the order is the argument and the plate of food is the returned value.

rows: Write the code once, call it many times

Each function can be checked separately
Different students can write different functions
A correction in one function fixes every call

blocks.html: C++ has two kinds of functions: library (built-in) functions that come with the compiler, and user-defined functions that you write yourself.
Library functions are stored in header files. You include the header and call the function directly.

b) is an error.

blocks.html: C++ allows several functions to have the same name as long as their parameter lists differ — in the number of parameters or in their types. The compiler picks the right version by looking at the arguments. This is called function overloading. Functions cannot be overloaded on the return type alone.

blocks.html: The scope of a variable is the part of the program where it can be used.

items.html: A local variable is declared inside a function or block. It is created when the function starts and destroyed when it ends. Other functions cannot see it.
A global variable is declared outside all functions. Every function below it can use it, and it lives until the program ends.

blocks.html: Use global variables sparingly: because any function can change them, mistakes are hard to trace.

blocks.html: A function that calls itself is called a recursive function. Every recursive function needs:

items.html: a base case — a simple case answered directly, which stops the recursion; and
a recursive case — which calls the same function on a smaller problem.

blocks.html: Without a base case the function would call itself again and again until the program crashes.

blocks.html: Notice how short and readable main() is: each job lives in its own function.
Did you know? main() is itself a function. Its return type is int , and return 0; tells the operating system that the program finished successfully. A non-zero value is used to report an error.
